title: mixengine-artifact.json
description: Written into the root of every archive this repository publishes. It is the reason the daemon can install a borrowed artifact without knowing anything about how its publisher lays out a directory: the archive keeps that layout, and this file says where things are. An archive without one is not an artifact.

source.description: Whether the payload came from a publisher who already produces something relocatable, or was compiled here. It is recorded because the two age differently: a borrowed artifact goes stale when its publisher moves, a built one when its recipe stops compiling.

upstream.description: Where a borrowed payload came from, kept so a reader can check that what is in the archive is what upstream published — even after upstream has deleted it.

verified_against.description: What the hash was checked against — for PHP on Windows, windows.php.net's own releases.json rather than a hash we computed and then trusted.

project.description: Who published the payload, where that is not simply the runtime's own project: "astral-sh/python-build-standalone", "oneclick/rubyinstaller2".

release.description: The publisher's own identifier for the release this came out of, when it is not the runtime version. python-build-standalone tags by date and RubyInstaller tags by version *and packaging revision*, so two archives of one CPython or one Ruby are told apart here rather than in the index, which is keyed on the runtime version alone.

variant.description: Which asset of that release was taken, where the publisher offers several of the same target — python-build-standalone's `install_only_stripped` against its `install_only`.

added.description: Paths this repository wrote into an otherwise borrowed archive, so that a reader comparing it against upstream finds the difference stated rather than deducing it. There is one at the time of writing: Windows CPython archives get a `Scripts/pip.cmd`, because upstream ships the pip package with no entry point and a generated `pip.exe` would carry an absolute interpreter path into a tree that is going to move.

stripped.description: Set where an otherwise borrowed payload had its debug symbols removed, with what that saved — because an archive claiming to be stripped and weighing what an unstripped one weighs is a claim worth being able to check. MariaDB is why this exists: upstream's Linux bintar carries its symbols inside every binary, so the same server packed to 371 MB from the bintar and 27 MB from upstream's own .deb packages, which Debian strips.

removed.description: Paths taken *out* of an otherwise borrowed archive, for the same reason `added` states the ones put in. Two things are removed. One is a file that would make the archive work on some machines and not others: Linux CPython before 3.13 ships a `_crypt` module linked against a libxcrypt no archive here carries, which is present on Debian and Ubuntu and absent on a default Fedora, and deleting it is what lets `smoke.relocated` keep meaning that nothing in the tree reaches outside it. The other is a feature the publisher shipped unevenly, which is how one version comes to mean two things — either to one platform and not the other, as every Node.js tarball carries 59 MB of C++ headers that no Windows zip has ever carried and that `node-gyp` does not read; or to both platforms in different forms, as CPython carries Tk 8.6 with Tix on Windows and Tk 9.0 with itcl on Unix. A directory removed whole is named by its root — `include`, rather than the 2,726 files under it — so that six cells of one version stay comparable field to field.

changed.description: Files that ship at the path upstream published them and are *not the bytes upstream published*, mapped to the command that made them different. This is the hardest difference for a reader holding both archives to account for, because it is the one that looks like a corrupted download rather than a decision. There is one at the time of writing: `strip --strip-all` on Linux and `strip -x` on macOS, over every ELF and Mach-O in a CPython tree. Upstream's `install_only_stripped` removed the debug information and nothing else, which left the symbol tables — and, from 3.12 on, 6.5 MB of `.rela.text` in `lib/libpython3.X.so.1.0`, relocations emitted so that BOLT could run and then never used, since the `.note.bolt_info` proving BOLT ran is in `bin/python3.X` and in no library. Windows cells never carry this field: their stripped variant ships no `.pdb` at all, which is what the other two are being levelled down to. The flag differs by object format on purpose — ELF's `.dynsym` is a second, allocated table a strip may not touch, while Mach-O keeps one table whose exported range `--strip-all` empties.

recipe.description: For a built payload: the tool and version that produced it, e.g. "static-php-cli 2.7.1". Also set on a borrowed payload this repository added something compiled to — PHP on Windows names the PECL release of each extension it downloaded, because that is the same fact the Unix recipes record about the ones they compiled, and a reader comparing two cells of one version should find it spelled the same way on both.

keeps.description: Paths this artifact carries that *One version means one thing, and no more than is needed* would otherwise throw out — headers, import libraries, manual pages, test suites — mapped to why each one is needed here. Unlike `upstream.added` and `upstream.removed` this states no difference from the publisher; it states a difference from this repository's own rule, which is why it sits at the top level and applies to a built artifact as much as to a borrowed one. It is a mapping rather than a list because a check reading a bare path can only report that something was declared, and the point of declaring is that the reason travels with the artifact. CPython is why it exists: `pip install` of a source distribution compiles a C extension on the machine doing the installing, against `include/` and — on Windows, where an extension cannot leave Python's symbols undefined — linked to `libs/python3XX.lib`. The same file type is deleted from the PHP archives, which reach a developer as DLLs somebody else compiled; "needed" is a question about the runtime, not about the extension. An entry may also record something no per-artifact check would ever flag, and CPython has the largest of those too: a `lib/libpython3.X.so` that nothing in the tree loads, kept because the interpreter's own `python3-config` hands an embedder a link line naming it — a reason nobody could reconstruct from the file, which is the case this field is most worth writing for.

lacks.description: What this cell cannot do that the other cells of the same version can, mapped to why — the one field here that is an admission rather than a decision, and it is written because the alternative is an artifact that is quietly less than its version number promises. Everything else in this repository resolves an asymmetry by moving one side; this is for the asymmetries that cannot be moved at any price. Ruby on Windows is why it exists and holds both entries at the time of writing: RubyInstaller builds `x64-mingw-ucrt`, which CRuby does not build YJIT for, while the four compiled cells are configured `--enable-yjit` and refuse to publish a Ruby that answers false to `RubyVM::YJIT.enabled?`; and `gem install` of a gem with a C extension exits 1 with `MSYS2 could not be found`, because the compiler is a separate ~1 GB toolchain published as its own installer. A daemon can read this and refuse to enable a feature the cell does not have, instead of passing a flag that warns; a blueprint asking for a native gem can fail where it is written rather than on somebody's machine. Absent means nothing is missing, which is why the recipes that lack nothing still ask and write no field at all rather than an empty one.

examples.yjit: RubyInstaller builds x64-mingw-ucrt, which CRuby does not build YJIT for.

enabled.description: Which of `shared` the daemon is expected to switch on, as opposed to merely offer. It exists because one version has to mean one thing across six cells and the two systems cannot say it the same way: curl, openssl, mbstring, intl, gd, zip, sodium, sqlite3 and fileinfo are compiled into the Unix builds and are loadable modules on Windows, where no build with them static exists — so `shared` listed them beside `odbc` and said "available" about both. `static` ∪ `enabled` is what an artifact actually does, and it is the set that has to match across the cells of a version; `static` ∪ `shared` is only what it could be asked to do. Empty on the 8.1+ Unix builds, where everything is compiled in and the one loadable module is a debugger nobody wants running by default.

smoke.description: What was actually proven about this archive before it was published, on the machine that built it. `php -v` alone is not enough: it passes with a broken extension_dir, because the built-in extensions are static and never consult it.

relocated.description: The archive was extracted, moved to an unrelated directory, and exercised from there — never from where it was produced.

openssl.description: The TLS library the archive was proven to *call*, as it names itself. Recorded because it is the one thing about a bundled runtime a user cannot see from outside, and because every runtime here carries its own: a Python, a Ruby and a Node.js installed on one machine are three different OpenSSLs.

loaded_extension.description: A shared extension that was loaded from extension_dir after relocation. Written by no recipe since P2 — PHP on Windows was the last one proving a single extension, and it now proves all of them under `loaded_extensions` like the other two. Kept here because artifacts published before that carry it.

loaded_extensions.description: Every shared extension that was loaded after relocation, where the recipe proves all of them rather than one. Proving one shows extension_dir is honoured; proving all shows no extension built into an archive that cannot load it — which is a separate failure, invisible in a build log, and the usual shape of it is an extension whose symbols come from another extension that has to be loaded first.
